title: Vicky Kaushal Just Blocked 18 Months of His Life for One Role — and It Starts Now
excerpt: The actor wraps Love and War and walks straight into six months of physical transformation for Mahavatar, where he'll play the axe-wielding immortal Parashurama. No other films. No distractions. Just the character.
body:
There's ambition, and then there's what **Vicky Kaushal** is about to do.

As *Love and War* — the sweeping Sanjay Leela Bhansali drama co-starring **Ranbir Kapoor** and **Alia Bhatt** — wraps its final 50-day schedule this month, Kaushal won't be taking a holiday. He won't be signing his next three-film deal. He won't be showing up at brand events in sharp suits.

Instead, starting this month, Vicky Kaushal disappears. For eighteen months. Into the body, the mind, and the mythology of **Chiranjeevi Parashurama** — the immortal warrior-sage of Hindu scripture, the axe-wielding sixth avatar of Lord Vishnu.

The film is **Mahavatar**. The director is **Amar Kaushik**. The banner is **Maddock Films**. And the commitment is unlike anything we've seen from a Bollywood A-lister in recent memory.

## The Transformation Begins

According to a Pinkvilla exclusive, Vicky has entered an **intensive six-month preparation phase** that kicked off in June 2026. This isn't your standard "hit the gym for three weeks and post shirtless photos" Bollywood prep. Amar Kaushik has designed a comprehensive training module that covers physical transformation — the kind of bulking-up that rewires how a body moves — alongside acting workshops that dig into the psychological and emotional architecture of the character.


![Sanjay Leela Bhansali — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9a/Sanjay_Leela_Bhansali.jpg)


> "Amar has designed a very detailed prep module for Vicky. It's not just about the physicality, but also about getting into the psychological and emotional graph of the character." — Source, Pinkvilla

Parashurama isn't a simple strongman role. In Hindu mythology, he's one of the seven Chiranjeevis — the immortals who still walk the earth. He's a Brahmin who chose the warrior's path, a figure defined by both devastating rage and profound spiritual discipline. Playing him demands someone who can hold fury and stillness in the same frame.

If there's a working actor in Bollywood right now who can do that, it's Vicky Kaushal.



> **"This isn't your standard "hit the gym for three weeks and post shirtless photos" Bollywood prep."**


https://www.instagram.com/p/DZg12ubiFih/


## No Other Films. Period.

Here's the detail that turns this from impressive to genuinely rare: **Vicky will not take on any other film during the entire Mahavatar commitment.** Principal photography is slated to run from **January 2027 through December 2027** — a full year of shooting, with the six months of prep before it.


![Lord Vishnu — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ef/Vishnu_from_Gita_Govinda.jpg)


> "Vicky is treating Mahavatar as a once-in-a-lifetime project. He wants to be fully invested, which is why he has consciously decided not to take up any other assignments during the shoot." — Source, Pinkvilla

In an industry where top stars routinely juggle four or five films simultaneously, where dates are the currency that determines who gets cast in what, an actor voluntarily locking himself out of every other opportunity for eighteen months is almost radical. It's the kind of decision that either produces a career-defining masterpiece or becomes a cautionary tale about betting everything on one card.

Vicky is betting it produces a masterpiece.

## The Amar Kaushik Factor

**Amar Kaushik** has never directed anything like this. He built his reputation on the *Stree* franchise and *Bhediya* — films that blend horror, comedy, and Indian folklore with a commercial sensibility that's become Maddock Films' signature. *Mahavatar* represents a dramatic gear shift: from contemporary horror-comedy to full-blown mythological epic.

But there's a logic to it. Kaushik has always understood how Indian mythology lives in the popular imagination — as campfire stories, as grandmother's warnings, as village truths that modernity hasn't quite killed. *Stree* worked because it treated its folklore with both reverence and wit. *Mahavatar* drops the wit and leans fully into the reverence, but the instinct — that Indian mythological stories deserve to be told with scale and emotional truth, not just spectacle — carries over.


![Amar Kaushik — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/98/The_Director_Amar_Khaushik_of_the_film_AABA%2C_at_the_Presentation%2C_during_the_48th_International_Film_Festival_of_India_%28IFFI-2017%29%2C_in_Panaji%2C_Goa_on_November_27%2C_2017.jpg)


The first-look posters, unveiled last year on Parashuram Jayanti, showed Kaushal in full warrior mode: **long hair, thick beard, fiery visuals**, and an intensity that suggested this isn't going to be a glossy comic-book interpretation. This is going to be raw.

## Where the Diaspora Comes In

For NRI audiences, Indian mythological cinema has been a complicated category. The old Doordarshan serials carry deep nostalgia, but the modern Bollywood attempts have been uneven. *Adipurush* promised and disappointed. *Brahmastra* built a universe but left the mythology feeling thin.

*Mahavatar* could be different. Parashurama is a figure who resonates across the diaspora — particularly among audiences who grew up with the stories of the Dashavatara, the ten avatars of Vishnu. A film that treats that material with genuine seriousness and an actor who physically transforms to embody it is the kind of project that sells itself.

Maddock Films is reportedly planning a **grand pan-India release**, likely in 2028. Multiple-language distribution seems certain. For the diaspora, this could be the kind of event cinema that turns a regular Thursday night at the AMC into something that feels like a homecoming.

## The Bigger Picture

Vicky Kaushal's trajectory from *Masaan* to *Uri* to *Sardar Udham* to *Sam Bahadur* to *Chhaava* has been one of the most impressive career arcs in modern Bollywood. Each role has been physically and emotionally bigger than the last. *Mahavatar* is the logical next step — and possibly the most dangerous one, because the mythology comes with devotional weight that no amount of good acting can protect you from if the film misreads its tone.

But if Kaushal and Kaushik get this right? If they can make Parashurama feel as real and raw and devastating as the source material promises?

Eighteen months will have been a bargain.
